newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: TERRITORY SHOULD HELP LAST TWO PEOPLE TO DIE: PERRON
Former Northern Territory Chief Minister Marshall Perron says Territory authorities should indemnify from prosecution anyone assisting two terminally ill people to die.
The two had qualified for access to the Territory Right To Die law, but had not done so before it was overturned by the Federal Parliament.
Mr Perron says the Territory would be adopting the approach in Holland where doctors administering euthanasia are not prosecuted providing they have complied with the set of guidelines.
Mr Perron, who drafted the Territory's law, says the two patients had their rights removed by the passage of the Andrews Bill and deserve justice and dignity.
BEAZLEY WARNS QLD PREMIER TO FOLLOW CONVENTION
The leader of the Federal Opposition, Kim Beazley, has warned Queensland's Premier there will be electoral consequences if he fails to appoint a Labor politician if Senator Colston resigns.
Mr Beazley says he expects to have an input into the decision and says the Queensland Premier, the National Party's Rob Borbidge, should act within a couple of days of a resignation.
He says it will be to Mr Borbidge's detriment to act in any other way.
BANK WORKERS WILL TAKE ACTION IF JOBS GO IN MERGERS
Industrial action by bank employees could be one of the side-effects of the Wallis inquiry into Australia's financial sector.
The inquiry lifted the ban on mergers between the big four banks, but Treasurer Peter Costello says no mergers will be allowed, for the time being.
The Finance Sector Union has warned banks and the Government that mergers have cost over 30-thousand jobs in the past five years, and workers aren't prepared to take any more.
Secretary, Tony Beck, says Mr Costello's assurance falls short of being a long-term commitment.
Mr Beck says employees don't trust the banks any more, and will be prepared to take strong action to defend their jobs.
WARNING ABOUT PERILS OF RELAXING MEDIA OWNERSHIP RULES
A major study of the commercial radio industry is warning of the consequences of relaxing media ownership regulations.

The study - from the Communications Law Centre - documents the last decade of the industry under cross-media rules, where one-third of journalists have lost their jobs and ownership has been concentrated.
The Federal Government is currently reviewing media ownership.
The study will be presented at a major conference on media ownership in Sydney today, to be opened by the Federal Communications Minister, Richard Alston.
DROUGHT SPREADS IN NSW
There's been an eight per-cent increase in the area of New South Wales affected by drought.
Twenty-seven percent of the state has been drought-declared for April following a lack of significant rainfall over much of the southern half of New South Wales during March.
The new drought declared areas are the whole of the Condoblin Rural Lands Protection Board and parts of the Young, Forbes, Molong, Hay, Hillston, Cobar and Bourke boards.
